title: Plotinus in modern English
author: Plotinus
label: The Workshop's modern English, machine-assisted: drafted with an AI model (Claude) from the Greek and not yet checked by a scholar. Taylor's English of each chapter is one tap away.
about: A modern English version of Plotinus, written for the Workshop. It is translated from the Greek of Volkmann's edition (Leipzig, 1883-1884), as First1KGreek gives it, chapter by chapter, and checked against Thomas Taylor's translation of 1817. Where the Greek says something Taylor's English does not, the modern version follows the Greek, and a flag shows Taylor's words and the difference. Plato's words that Plotinus quotes are noted with their place. The chapters are Volkmann's (Ficino's); the short titles and summaries are the Workshop's. So far: Ennead I.2, On the Virtues, and I.3, On Dialectic, the first of the treatises in Porphyry's order that Taylor translated.

treatises.title: On the virtues
treatises.summary: Plato says we should escape from this world by becoming like God, through virtue. But God has no need of virtues. Plotinus answers that we can become like something that does not itself have what makes us like it, as a house is like the plan of it. He then sets the virtues in two ranks: the civic virtues, which put measure into our desires and feelings, and the greater virtues, which purify the soul and turn it to intellect. The good person lives by the greater, and his aim is to live the life of the gods, not just the life of a good human being.

treatises.title: On dialectic
treatises.summary: What leads us up to the Good? Plato names three kinds of people who can be led up: the musician, the lover and the philosopher. Each starts from a different place, and Plotinus says how each is to be led. All of them must come at last to dialectic, which is not a tool for arguing but the highest part of philosophy: knowledge of what each thing is, which rests in the intelligible world and hands logic over to others. The lower virtues and wisdom grow together and complete each other.

treatises.title: On matter
treatises.summary: Everyone who has thought about matter agrees that it is a substrate, a receiver of forms; they differ about what it is. Plotinus first argues that there is a matter in the intelligible world too: the depth beneath the forms there, unbounded until it turns to the One. He then turns to the matter of bodies. It is needed because the elements change into one another; it has no quality and no size, and is known only by a "bastard reasoning". It is not a quality, nor a privation added to something else: it is the unlimited itself, poverty itself, and so evil.

treatises.title: Against the Gnostics
treatises.summary: Against those who say the maker of the world is evil and the world is bad: the Gnostics among Plotinus' own hearers. There are three principles and no more: the Good, intellect and soul. The world was not made by a soul that fell, nor by reasoning, but by soul's contemplation of what is above it; it is the best possible image of the intelligible world, and the stars have souls better than ours. The Gnostics borrow from Plato and spoil what they borrow, multiply beings, despise the gods, claim to be the only sons of God, offer magic for cures, and teach no virtue. The good person lives here calmly, as in a fine house built by another.

treatises.title: On the impassibility of things without body
treatises.summary: How can the soul, which has no body, be free from affection, when it seems to feel pleasure and pain, fear and desire, and to change with virtue and vice? Plotinus answers that perception, memory and virtue are activities, not imprints; the feelings belong to the body or to the living compound, with soul as their cause; and purification is the soul's waking from images. Then matter: it too is untouched. It is not being but a phantom, a mirror in which images come and go and leave no trace, "the receptacle and nurse" of becoming, which takes on nothing and keeps nothing.

chapters.title: Becoming like God: does God have virtues?
chapters.summary: We escape evil by becoming like God. But which god, and does he have the virtues? The world-soul, who has nothing to fear and nothing to desire, cannot have courage or self-control. Then we are made like what does not have virtue: as the house we see is like the house in the mind, which has no need of order.

chapters.title: Two kinds of likeness; the civic virtues
chapters.summary: Likeness is of two kinds: between two copies of one original, and between a copy and its original. The civic virtues give measure to our desires and feelings, and so carry a trace of the measure above; the soul, nearer to the divine than the body, can seem a god itself.

chapters.title: The greater virtues are purifications
chapters.summary: Plato calls the virtues purifications, so there are two kinds. The soul is bad when it is mixed up with the body; it is good when it thinks on its own, does not share the body's feelings, does not fear to leave it, and lets reason lead. This is likeness to God. But God is not in a state of virtue: virtue belongs to the soul, not to intellect or what is beyond it.

chapters.title: Purification, turning, and the soul's own good
chapters.summary: Is virtue the purifying, or the having been purified? Purification only removes what is foreign; the soul's good is to be with what is akin to it, and it reaches it by turning. Its virtue is what comes from the turning: a seeing of the realities, whose imprints the soul held unlit and now lights up.

chapters.title: How far purification goes
chapters.summary: The purified soul draws itself together away from the body. It takes bodily pleasures only as cures, bears pain calmly, removes anger and fear as far as it can, and desires nothing base. It wants to make its lower part pure too, so that this part respects reason, as a man respects a wise neighbour.

chapters.title: To be a god, not only without fault
chapters.summary: The aim is not to be free from fault but to be a god. In the purified person wisdom is the seeing of what intellect holds. Each virtue is twofold: in intellect it is not virtue but the pattern; in the soul it is virtue. The greater justice, self-control and courage are the soul's activity towards intellect, its turning inward, and its freedom from passion.

chapters.title: The virtues follow one another; the life of the gods
chapters.summary: The virtues go together in the soul, as their patterns do in intellect. Whoever has the greater virtues has the lesser ones in potential. The good person will use the lesser when circumstances call for them, but will live by the higher measures, and choose not the life of a good human being but the life of the gods.

chapters.title: Who can be led up, and the musician
chapters.summary: The journey has two stages: up to the intelligible world, and then through it to its summit. Plato names three natures fit for the first: the musician, the lover and the philosopher. The musician, stirred by beautiful sounds, must be taught that what moved him was the harmony and beauty of the intelligible world.

chapters.title: The lover
chapters.summary: The lover remembers beauty but cannot grasp it apart from bodies. He must be led, as in Plato's Symposium, from one beautiful body to all of them, then to beautiful ways of life and laws, arts, sciences and virtues, and from the virtues up to intellect and being.

chapters.title: The philosopher
chapters.summary: The philosopher by nature is already winged and moving upward, and needs only to be shown the way: first mathematics, to train him in thinking of what has no body; then the completion of his virtues; then dialectic.

chapters.title: What dialectic is
chapters.summary: Dialectic is the power to say of each thing what it is, how it differs from others and what it shares with them, and to do this by knowledge, not opinion. It works in the intelligible world, dividing and combining the Forms until it reaches the first principle; then it rests, and leaves logic to another art.

chapters.title: Where dialectic gets its principles; dialectic and philosophy
chapters.summary: Intellect gives dialectic its principles. Dialectic is the most valuable part of philosophy, not a tool: it deals with real things, judges falsehood by the truth it holds, and leaves the fine points of propositions to another art.

chapters.title: The other parts of philosophy, and the natural virtues
chapters.summary: Philosophy also studies nature and conduct, with help from dialectic. Practical wisdom reasons about the virtues as a whole; dialectic and wisdom serve it from above. The lower virtues are incomplete without wisdom, and wisdom cannot come without them: the two grow together.

chapters.title: What the schools say matter is
chapters.summary: All agree that matter is a substrate and a receiver of forms, but not what it is. The Stoics, who hold that only bodies exist, make matter the one substance under the elements, a body without quality, and even make God matter in a certain state. Others call it incorporeal, and some posit a second matter in the intelligible world, under the forms there.

chapters.title: Objections to a matter in the intelligible world
chapters.summary: If matter is unbounded and formless, it cannot be among the best things there; simple things need no matter; only things that come to be need it. And where would it come from? If it was made, something made it; if it is eternal, there are many first principles; and form added to it would make a body there.

chapters.title: The unbounded is not always to be despised
chapters.summary: Not everything unbounded and shapeless is to be scorned, if it offers itself to what is better, as soul does to intellect. Composition there is not like that of bodies. The matter of things that come to be takes one form after another; the matter there has all forms at once, and so is never without form.

chapters.title: Why there must be matter there
chapters.summary: If there are many Forms, they have something in common and something of their own; what is their own is their shape, and what is shaped is matter. The world here imitates that world, and this one is made of matter, so that one has matter too. Take away from intellect its variety, shapes and thoughts, and what is left before them is shapeless and unbounded.

chapters.title: The depth of each thing; the matter there
chapters.summary: Intellect divides each thing till it reaches what is simple; the depth of each is matter, and so all matter is dark. The matter there has a defined and thinking life; the matter here becomes a defined but dead thing. The matter there comes from Otherness, the first motion, which is unbounded until it turns to the One and is lit by it.

chapters.title: Why bodies need a substrate
chapters.summary: The elements change into one another, so something must remain under the change: what perishes is never wholly destroyed, and nothing comes from what wholly is not. Perishing, induction and analysis all show that bodies are composite, of matter and form. The elements are not form alone, nor first matter, so they are made of both.

chapters.title: Against Empedocles, Anaxagoras, the infinite and atoms
chapters.summary: Empedocles' elements perish, so they are not matter. Anaxagoras' mixture, which has everything already, does away with the intellect he brings in. The infinite cannot be matter, whether as a thing by itself or as an attribute of a body. Atoms do not exist, since every body can be divided, and nothing continuous or living could be made of them.

chapters.title: Matter has no quality and no size
chapters.summary: Matter is not a body, since a body has quality. Being the matter of all sensible things, it has none of their properties: no colour, heat, weight or shape, and no size either. It must be simple. The forming principle brings size with it, as it brings quality; for each kind the form fixes its size.

chapters.title: Quantity is a form
chapters.summary: Not everything that exists has size: nothing incorporeal does, and matter is incorporeal. Quantity itself is not a quantity; what shares in it is. As what makes a thing white is not white, what makes a thing so big is not so big but the principle of size. It does not unroll matter into size; it gives it size it did not have.

chapters.title: How matter is thought: a bastard reasoning
chapters.summary: How can we think what has no size and no quality? By a kind of unboundedness in the soul, as darkness is the eye's matter. The account of it is bounded, but the soul's grasp of it is not; so its image is "bastard", as Plato says. The soul thinks it dimly, by not thinking, and quickly puts form on it again, afraid of being outside the things that are.

chapters.title: Matter is not bulk, but has a phantom of bulk
chapters.summary: Some say that if matter has no size it contributes nothing, and bodies need no matter. But a receiver need not have bulk: soul receives everything without it. Matter receives its forms in extension because it can receive extension. It has a phantom of bulk: great and small at once, running from one to the other, which is why some called it the void.

chapters.title: Matter is needed, and known by reasoning, not sense
chapters.summary: Forms of bodies are in sizes, but about something sized, other than size; otherwise there would be only rational principles in soul, and no bodies. Actions need no matter, but bodies are composite. So matter is not an empty name. It is grasped by no sense, but by an empty reasoning, a bastard one; and it has no bodiliness either.

chapters.title: Matter is not a quality, not even a privation
chapters.summary: If the substrate were a common quality, how could a quality be a substrate? Someone says matter is qualified by having no quality, as a blind man is qualified by blindness. But privation is not a quality; it is an absence, like silence. Matter's own character is just what it is: to be other than everything else, or rather "others".

chapters.title: Is matter privation?
chapters.summary: Is matter privation, or is privation in matter? Some say they are one in substrate, two in account. Then each account must be given. If they are separate, they are two; if like the snub nose, or fire and heat, they are still not one. If privation is a not-being, still there are two accounts. But if to be matter is to be unbounded and without quality, how are there two?

chapters.title: Matter is the unbounded itself
chapters.summary: The unbounded is not an attribute of matter: what orders is limit and principle, so what is ordered must be the unlimited, and an attribute must be a principle. So matter is the unlimited itself. In the intelligible world it is born of the One's infinite power; the matter here, an image fleeing from true being, is more truly unlimited.

chapters.title: Matter is poverty, and so evil
chapters.summary: Matter is not Otherness itself, but the part of Otherness opposed to the true beings, and so it is not-being and privation. Form coming to it does not destroy it, but brings it to what it is, as a seed sown or a female made pregnant. It is evil, not because it wants the good, but because it is poverty itself: of wisdom, virtue, beauty and form.

chapters.title: Three principles, and no more
chapters.summary: The Good is simple and first, the same as the One, with nothing above it. After it comes intellect, then soul: no fewer, since they differ, and no more. There is no intellect at rest beside one in motion, nor one that thinks beside one that thinks that it thinks, nor a rational principle between intellect and soul.

chapters.title: One intellect; and our soul in three parts
chapters.summary: There is one intellect, always the same, imitating its father as far as it can. Part of our soul is always with the things there, part with the things here, and part between; the lower part can drag down the middle, but not the whole. The soul of the universe never fell: it orders the world without effort, by looking at what is above it.

chapters.title: Everything gives of itself: the world has no beginning
chapters.summary: Lit always, soul always gives light to what follows, as a fire warms what is round it. Every principle must give of itself to another, or the Good would not be good, nor intellect intellect. So all things follow one another always: what is called "made" was always being made, and will not perish. Matter too is always lit.

chapters.title: The world-soul did not fall
chapters.summary: If they say the soul made the world when it lost its wings, the soul of the universe suffers no such thing. If it erred, when, and why then? It made the world not by sinking, but by not sinking; a forgetful soul could not make, and one that remembers would go back. Nor is the world badly made because it has much that is hard; it is the best image of the intelligible that there could be.

chapters.title: They rank themselves above the stars
chapters.summary: It is unreasonable for people who have bodies and passions to claim to touch the intelligible, and deny that the sun's soul is better than theirs, or that the heavens share in immortality. Their soul made of the elements cannot live. They hate the world and dream of a "new earth" as its pattern; but where would this pattern come from?

chapters.title: What is new in them is not true
chapters.summary: Their "sojourns", "antitypes" and "repentances" are empty words to found a sect. What is true in them they took from Plato; what is new is false. They misread the Timaeus and multiply intelligible beings. They should take from the ancients what is well said, argue fairly where they differ, and not abuse the Greeks to win a name.

chapters.title: The world-soul is not bound as we are
chapters.summary: The world never began and will not end. Our soul's union with the body is not best for it; but to judge the soul of the universe by ours is like blaming a whole city for its potters. We are bound by the body; the world-soul binds and is not bound, and orders its body without effort. What perishes is like a tortoise caught in a great dance.

chapters.title: The world is a clear image of the intelligible gods
chapters.summary: To ask why soul made the world is to ask why soul exists: it assumes a beginning to what is eternal. The world shows the greatness of the intelligible, a clear and beautiful statue of the intelligible gods; it had to exist, since the intelligible acts both in itself and on another. The stars are gods with virtue; and if souls came here willingly, why blame the place?

chapters.title: Wealth, poverty and wrongdoing; the many gods
chapters.summary: The good man does not seek equality in wealth or power. Wrongdoing comes from souls like children, not from intellect; and there are judgments and punishments here, and gods who watch. We should try to be as good as we can, but not think ourselves the only good ones: there are good daemons and gods, and the world-soul. God's greatness is shown in the many gods he makes. The Gnostics flatter fools: "you are a son of God".

chapters.title: Why Plotinus writes; the fall of Wisdom
chapters.summary: Much more could be examined, but Plotinus writes for his own pupils, out of regard for friends still held by these views, not to persuade the Gnostics. He ends with the most absurd thing: their story that soul and a certain "Wisdom" sank down and lit up the darkness, and that from images of images came the maker of this world.

chapters.title: The image that made the world
chapters.summary: If the soul did not come down but only lit the darkness, how did it sink? Why did it alone shine, and not the higher powers? Why did it wait for images to be born? An image of soul would need no matter. Is the image a substance or a "thought"? Either way, their story of a maker made of images falls apart.

chapters.title: How could an image remember, or plan?
chapters.summary: Their image, just born, could not remember what it never saw; yet they, true souls, scarcely recollect. Nature does not make fire first and then the rest, but outlines the whole animal at once. Foreseeing the heavens and the zodiac is no work of an image. If the lighting of the darkness was natural, it was always; if not, evil was there before the world, and the cause goes back to the first.

chapters.title: Do not fear the spheres
chapters.summary: Whoever blames the world does not know the order of first, second and third. The spheres are not terrors, as the Gnostics' tragedies make them, but bring good things; their bodies are fine and their souls finer. What they do are signs of things to come. Not all can be good; what is less good is not therefore evil, or there would be evil in the intelligible world too.

chapters.title: Magic, and diseases as daemons
chapters.summary: They make the higher beings open to spells, as if words and hissings could charm what is incorporeal. They say diseases are daemons they can drive out; but diseases have bodily causes, and are cured by purging, bleeding and fasting. Our philosophy, by contrast, shows simplicity of character and pure thinking, with dignity, not arrogance.

chapters.title: They teach no virtue
chapters.summary: Of the two schools of the end of life, pleasure and the beautiful, the Gnostics are worse than Epicurus: he removed providence, but they blame its lord, mock the laws and self-control, and leave only pleasure. They say nothing about virtue, what it is or how the soul is purified. "Look to God" helps nothing without being taught how; without true virtue, God is only a name.

chapters.title: To despise the world is not to be good
chapters.summary: Despising the world and its gods does not make anyone good; one who loves the father loves his children too. They say God cares for them alone, but if he is absent from the world he is absent from them. The universe is ordered and wise; no musician or geometer is unmoved by the image of the intelligible he sees here, and whoever is unmoved by the beauty of the stars has not seen the beauty there.

chapters.title: The beauty of the world, inside and out
chapters.summary: If they hate the body because Plato blamed it, they should take the body away in thought and see the intelligible sphere and the souls that give it size. The world-soul gives body all the beauty it can take, without jealousy. Despise the beauty of boys and women if you must, but not the beauty of the whole: the universe was never a child, and nothing bad can be added to it.

chapters.title: Two men in one fine house
chapters.summary: They say their teaching makes people flee the body, and ours keeps the soul in it. It is like two men in a fine house: one finds fault with it and stays; the other praises the builder and waits calmly for the time to leave. We should live in our bodies as the world-soul lives in the whole, untroubled; and not grudge the stars their contemplation, as though they did not see because we do not see their souls.

chapters.title: Can the soul be affected?
chapters.summary: Perceptions are not affections but activities and judgments about them. But how is the soul unchanged, when vice, false opinions, pleasures, pains and desires seem to arise in it? If soul has no size and is to be imperishable, we must not give it such affections; we must think of them as "affections without affection", taken over from bodies by analogy.

chapters.title: Virtue and vice are not alterations
chapters.summary: Virtue is a harmony of the soul's parts, vice a discord; but each part has its own virtue first. Ignorance is an absence; false opinion is like a false sight. Reason "hears" intellect as sight sees: the activity is no alteration. Memory too is a power woken, not a store of imprints. Cowardice, courage and licence are ways each part acts or fails to act, with no change in its substance.

chapters.title: Feelings belong to the body; their source is in soul
chapters.summary: We cannot deny that pleasure, pain, fear and desire are real changes; but we must ask what changes. To say the soul blushes or turns pale would be absurd: the shame or fear begins in soul, the blood changes in the body. Soul's movements come from it, as life does, without alteration; memories and images are not stamped in it like wax.

chapters.title: The affective part is a form, like a harmony
chapters.summary: The affective part is where feelings followed by pleasure and pain arise. Some follow opinion, some come before it. The image in soul starts the trouble, but the trembling and pallor are in the body. The affective part is a form in matter, rooted in the soul of growth; it moves the body as a harmony might move the strings, itself unmoved.

chapters.title: Then why purify the soul?
chapters.summary: If the soul is not affected, why make it free from affection by philosophy? Because the image coming into it is followed by trouble; reason would remove the image, as waking ends a dream. Purification is to leave the soul alone, not looking to other things or holding alien opinions; for the lower part, it is waking from strange images and not leaning down.

chapters.title: Being, and the bodies that seem most real
chapters.summary: Now matter. First, true being is not what most people think: it lacks nothing, is life and intellect, receives nothing, and is all things at once. Bodies and their substrate are not-being. Hard things seem most real because they strike us, but the heavier a thing, the more it falls short; perceiving is the sleep of the soul, and true waking is a rising from bodies.

chapters.title: Matter is a phantom, a mirror of images
chapters.summary: Matter is incorporeal, but not soul, intellect, life, form or power: it is truly not-being, a phantom of bulk, invisible, seen when one does not look. What seems to be in it are images in an image, as in a mirror; they come and go and do nothing to it, as forms might pass through a void. So it stays unaffected.

chapters.title: What is affected must have opposites in it
chapters.summary: What is affected must have qualities opposite to those that come upon it, as heat is altered by cold. When fire perishes, the fire perishes, not the matter; affection is the road to perishing, and matter cannot perish. But how can matter hold so many mingled qualities and not be affected with them?

chapters.title: Things can be present without affecting
chapters.summary: One thing can be present in another in several ways: changing it, improving it without affecting it, or like a shape in wax, or light, which alters nothing. Mirrors are not affected by their images; matter is even less. Only opposites affect opposites; matter has no opposite in it, so it is like a house in which men fight, untouched by the blows.

chapters.title: If matter were altered, it would not stay matter
chapters.summary: If matter were affected, it would keep something of the affection, and become qualified matter, and then many-shaped, no longer able to receive everything, and so perishable. What is altered must remain while it changes; so matter, whose being is to be matter, cannot be altered as matter, any more than a form can be altered in its substance.

chapters.title: How matter shares in form without being changed
chapters.summary: Plato's words, "the things that come in and go out are always imitations of the things that are", point to the puzzle: not how forms come into matter, but how they are in it while it stays unaffected. Matter gains nothing and loses nothing. If it were truly made beautiful it would cease to be matter; it shares only in seeming, and so stays evil, unaffected even by the good.

chapters.title: Plato's figures: matter is not altered by shapes
chapters.summary: Plato makes matter take on figures to show that it stays unaffected: if shapes cause the feelings of living bodies while matter has none, it is not altered by them. His words "burnt" and "made wet" are softened by "receiving the forms of air and water". Fire is not "burnt"; and what has no size cannot be divided.

chapters.title: Receptacle and nurse: matter keeps its nature
chapters.summary: They say matter flees from form; but matter is held in stones and rocks. It "flees" by being always itself, having form as if it never had it. Plato's "receptacle and nurse of all becoming", the "place" and "seat" in which things appear and from which they go, keep it unaffected. What comes into it is an image into what is not true, like a reflection in an invisible mirror.

chapters.title: Poverty, begging at the door
chapters.summary: Without matter, nothing would come to be, as there is no image without a mirror. Matter is the Poverty of Plato's myth: it begs, and takes whatever it is given, and is never filled; it lies with Resource, the wisdom of the image. What it seems to receive slides off it, like an echo, or like light on a burning-glass: it holds nothing and stays itself.

chapters.title: Images that do not mix
chapters.summary: The fire caught in a burning-glass is outside the glass and touches it; the forms are "outside" matter by its otherness alone, not mixing with it, as opinions and images in the soul come and go without mixing. But the soul can push its images away; matter, weaker, has nothing of its own, cannot even say "I am here", and is found only by a deep reasoning.

chapters.title: Size comes and goes, and matter stays
chapters.summary: A rational principle makes matter great by putting greatness round it; take the form away and the substrate is not great. The size of a horse goes with the horse; the size of fire with the fire. If the heaven and all in it ceased, all size would leave matter, which would remain as it was. Matter is all things by sharing, size among them.

chapters.title: The great runs out, and matter runs with it
chapters.summary: Matter is not size itself. The great in intellect and soul wants to be great, and gives its imitators the power to stamp it on another; running out in imaging, it drags matter with it, so that it seems great, stretched but not filled. Each principle images its own size into matter, which stretches to all, lying in the middle between form and nothing.

chapters.title: Like a cloak that can be taken off
chapters.summary: A thought of the great, with power to go outward, would meet a nature with no trace of form, and make it great as an image. Matter keeps its nature, wearing this greatness like a cloak it put on while running; take it off and it is as it was. Soul receives forms without bulk; matter, a shadow with no activity of its own, waits to suffer what the maker wills, and receives all things, but in parts.

chapters.title: The mother that does not beget
chapters.summary: What comes into matter, its "mother", neither harms nor helps it; qualities affect one another, and living bodies are affected, but matter stays. "Receptacle and nurse" suit it better than "mother", for it begets nothing. So the ancient wise men, in their rites, showed Hermes with the organ of generation, and the Mother of all with sterile attendants: matter receives, but does not beget.

paragraphs.modern: Evils are here, and they haunt this place by necessity, and the soul wants to escape evils. So we must escape from here. What, then, is the escape? "Becoming like God," Plato says. And this happens "if we become just and holy, with wisdom," and, in short, if we live in virtue. If, then, it is by virtue that we become like, are we made like someone who has virtue? And like which god? Is it the one who seems most of all to have these things, the soul of the world and the ruling power in it, which has a wonderful wisdom? It makes sense that we, being here, should become like this one. But first, it is open to question whether this one has all the virtues. Can it be self-controlled, or brave, when there is nothing it need fear, since nothing is outside it? And when nothing pleasant comes to it that it could desire when it is absent, so as to get it or seize it? But if it, too, reaches out towards the intelligible things that our souls reach for, then plainly our good order and our virtues also come to us from there.
paragraphs.greek: Ἐπειδὴ τὰ κακὰ ἐνταῦθα καὶ τόνδε τὸν τόπον περιπολεῖ ἐξ ἀνάγκης, βούλεται δὲ ἡ ψυχὴ φεύγειν τὰ κακά, φευκτέον ἐντεῦθεν. τίς οὖν ἡ φυγή; θεῷ, φησιν, ὁμοιωθῆναι. τοῦτο δέ, εἰ δίκαιοι καὶ ὅσιοι μετὰ φρονήσεως γενοίμεθα καὶ ὅλως ἐν ἀρετῇ. εἰ οὖν ἀρετῇ ὁμοιούμεθα, ἆρα ἀρετὴν ἔχοντι; καὶ δὴ καὶ τίνι ʽθεᾦ; ἆῤ οὖν τῷ μᾶλλον δοκοῦντι ταῦτα ἔχειν καὶ δὴ τῇ τοῦ κόσμου ψυχῇ καὶ τῷ ἐν ταύτῃ ἡγουμένῳ, ᾧ φρόνησις θαυμαστὴ ὑπάρχει; καὶ γὰρ εὔλογον ἐνταῦθα ὄντας τούτῳ ὁμοιοῦσθαι. ἢ πρῶτον μὲν ἀμφισβητήσιμον, εἰ καὶ τούτῳ ὑπάρχουσι πᾶσαι: οἷον σώφρονι ἢ ἀνδρείῳ εἶναι, ᾧ μήτε τι δεινόν ἐστιν: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἔξωθεν: μήτε προσιὸν ἡδύ, οὗ καὶ ἐπιθυμία ἂν γένοιτο μὴ παρόντος, ἵν’ ἔχῃ ἢ ἕλῃ. εἰ δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ ἐν ὀρέξει ἐστὶ τῶν νοητῶν, ὧν καὶ αἱ ἡμέτεραι, δῆλον ὅτι καὶ ἡμῖν ἐκεῖθεν ὁ κόσμος καὶ αἱ ἀρεταί.

flags.taylor: and to the intellect which is the leader in it
flags.why: The Greek says only "the ruling power in it"; Taylor names it intellect, as the later Platonists did.

notes: "Becoming like God" and "just and holy, with wisdom" are Plato's words in the Theaetetus (176a-b).

paragraphs.modern: Does that one have these virtues, then? It is surely not reasonable that it should have the virtues we call civic: practical wisdom, which belongs to the reasoning part; courage, which belongs to the spirited part; self-control, which lies in a kind of agreement and harmony of the desiring part with reason; and justice, which is each of these parts doing its own work, in ruling and being ruled. Then are we made like God not by the civic virtues, but by the greater ones that go by the same names? But if by others, are we not made like him at all by the civic ones? It would be unreasonable to say that we are not made like him by these in any way at all. At any rate tradition calls the people who have them godlike, and we must say that they have become like God in some way. But the likeness comes by the greater virtues. Either way, it follows that God has virtues, even if not virtues of this kind.
paragraphs.greek: ἆῤ οὖν ἐκεῖνο ταύτας ἔχει; ἢ οὐκ εὔλογον τάς γε πολιτικὰς λεγομένας ἀρετὰς ἔχειν, φρόνησιν μὲν περὶ τὸ λογιζόμενον, ἀνδρείαν δὲ περὶ τὸ θυμούμενον, σωφροσύνην δὲ ἐν ὁμολογίᾳ τινὶ καὶ συμφωνίᾳ ἐπιθυμητικοῦ πρὸς λογισμόν, δικαιοσύνην δὲ τὴν ἑκάστου τούτων ὁμοῦ οἰκειοπραγίαν ἀρχῆς πέρι καὶ τοῦ ἄρχεσθαι. ἆῤ οὖν οὐ κατὰ τὰς πολιτικὰς ὁμοιούμεθα, ἀλλὰ κατὰ τὰς μείζους τῷ αὐτῷ ὀνόματι χρωμένας; ἀλλ’ εἰ κατ’ ἄλλας, κατὰ τὰς πολιτικὰς ὅλως οὔ; ἢ ἄλογον μηδ’ ὁπωσοῦν ὁμοιοῦσθαι κατὰ ταύτας — τούτους γοῦν καὶ θείους ἡ φήμη λέγει καὶ λεκτέον ἀμηγέπη ὡμοιῶσθαι — κατὰ δὲ τὰς μείζους τὴν ὁμοίωσιν εἶναι. ἀλλ’ ἑκατέρως γε συμβαίνει ἀρετὰς ἔχειν κἂν εἰ μὴ τοιαύτας.

flags.taylor: For rumor also says, that these are divine
flags.why: The Greek says that tradition calls these men divine, that is, the people who have the civic virtues; Taylor makes it the virtues.

notes: The civic virtues and their parts of the soul are those of Plato's Republic (book 4, 441c-443b).

paragraphs.modern: Suppose, then, someone grants that we can be made like him, though we stand differently towards different virtues, and are not made like him by the civic ones. Then nothing stops us from becoming, by our own virtues, like one who has no virtue. How can this be? Like this. If something is warmed by the presence of heat, must the source of the heat also be warmed? And if something is hot by the presence of fire, must fire itself be warmed by the presence of fire? To the first, one might reply that there is heat in fire too, but heat that is part of its nature. So the argument, following the comparison, would make virtue something brought into the soul from outside, but natural to that from which the soul has it by imitation. To the argument from fire, one might reply that that one is virtue itself, and we hold it to be greater than virtue. But if what the soul shares in were the same as that from which it comes, we would have to speak in this way. As it is, the one is different from the other. The house we see is not the same as the intelligible house, though it has been made like it. The house we see shares in arrangement and order; but there, in the plan, there is no arrangement, no order, no proportion. In the same way we receive order, arrangement and agreement from there, and these belong to virtue here. But the things there have no need of agreement, order or arrangement, and so they have no need of virtue either. And we are none the less made like the things there by the presence of virtue. So much, then, to show that virtue need not be there because we are made like that world by virtue. But we must add persuasion to the argument, and not rest on force alone.
paragraphs.greek: εἰ οὖν τις συγχωρεῖ ὁμοιοῦσθαι δύνασθαι, ἄλλως ἡμῶν ἐχόντων πρὸς ἄλλας καὶ μὴ πρὸς τὰς πολιτικὰς ἀρετὰς ὡμοιωμένων, οὐδὲν κωλύει ἡμᾶς ταῖς αὑτῶν ἀρεταῖς ὁμοιοῦσθαι τῷ μὴ ἀρετὴν κεκτημένῳ. καὶ πῶς; ὧδε: εἴ τι θερμότητος παρουσίᾳ θερμαίνεται, ἀνάγκη καὶ ὅθεν ἡ θερμότης ἐλήλυθε θερμαίνεσθαι; καὶ εἴ τι πυρὸς παρουσίᾳ θερμόν ἐστιν, ἀνάγκη καὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτὸ πυρὸς παρουσίᾳ θερμαίνεσθαι; ἀλλὰ πρὸς μὲν τὸ πρότερον εἴποι ἄν τις καὶ ἐν τῷ πυρὶ εἶναι θερμότητα, ἀλλὰ σύμφυτον, ὥστε τὸν λόγον ποιεῖν τῇ ἀναλογίᾳ ἑπόμενον ἐπακτὸν μὲν τῇ ψυχῇ τὴν ἀρετήν, ἐκείνῳ δέ, ὅθεν μιμησαμένη ἔχει, σύμφυτον: πρὸς δὲ τὸν ἐκ τοῦ πυρὸς λόγον τὸ ἐκεῖνον ἀρετὴν εἶναι: ἀρετῆς δὲ ἀξιοῦμεν εἶναι μείζονα. ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν οὗ μεταλαμβάνει ψυχὴ τὸ αὐτὸ ἦν τῷ ἀφ̓ οὗ, οὕτως ἔδει λέγειν: νῦν δὲ ἕτερον μὲν ἐκεῖνο, ἕτερον δὲ τοῦτο. οὐδὲ γὰρ οἰκία ἡ αἰσθητὴ τὸ αὐτὸ τῇ νοητῇ, καίτοι ὡμοίωται: καὶ τάξεως δὲ καὶ κόσμου μεταλαμβάνει ἡ οἰκία ἡ αἰσθητὴ κἀκεῖ ἐν τῷ λόγῳ οὐκ ἔστι τάξις οὐδὲ κόσμος οὐδὲ συμμετρία. οὕτως οὖν κόσμου καὶ τάξεως καὶ ὁμολογίας μεταλαμβάνοντες ἐκεῖθεν καὶ τούτων ὄντων τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐνθάδε, οὐ δεομένων δὲ τῶν ἐκεῖ ὁμολογίας οὐδὲ κόσμου οὐδὲ τάξεως, οὐδ’ ἂν ἀρετῆς εἴη χρεία καὶ ὁμοιοίμεθα δὲ οὐδὲν ἧττον τοῖς ἐκεῖ δἰ ἀρετῆς παρουσίαν. πρὸς μὲν οὖν τὸ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον κἀκεῖ ἀρετὴν εἶναι, ἐπείπερ ἡμεῖς ἀρετῇ ὁμοιούμεθα, ταυτί: δεῖ δὲ πειθὼ ἐπάγειν τῷ λόγῳ μὴ μένοντας ἐπὶ τῆς βίας.

flags.taylor: but that virtue in him is in reality greater than virtue [because it subsists causally.]
flags.why: Taylor's words in square brackets are his own explanation, from the later Platonists; they are not in the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, we must take up the virtues by which we say we become like God. We want to find the one thing that, in us, is an imitation and is virtue, but there is a kind of original and is not virtue. Note that likeness is of two kinds. One kind requires something the same in the things that are alike: it holds between things made equally like each other from the same source. But where one thing is made like another, and that other comes first, does not stand in the same relation back to it, and is not called like it, likeness must be understood in another way. We do not require the same form in both, but rather a different one, since the likeness came about in this second way.
paragraphs.greek: πρῶτον τοίνυν τὰς ἀρετὰς ληπτέον, καθ̓ ἅς φαμεν ὁμοιοῦσθαι, ἵνα τὸ αὐτὸ εὕρωμεν, ὃ παῤ ἡμῖν μὲν μίμημα ὂν ἀρετή ἐστιν, ἐκεῖ δὲ οἷον ἀρχέτυπον ὂν οὐκ ἀρετή, ἐπισημηνάμενοι, ὡς ἡ ὁμοίωσις διττή: καὶ ἡ μέν τις ταὐτὸν ἐν τοῖς ὁμοίοις ἀπαιτεῖ, ὅσα ἐπίσης ὡμοίωται ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ: ἐν οἷς δὲ τὸ μὲν ὡμοίωται πρὸς ἕτερον, τὸ δὲ ἕτερόν ἐστι πρῶτον, οὐκ ἀντιστρέφον πρὸς ἐκεῖνο οὐδὲ ὅμοιον αὐτοῦ λεγόμενον, ἐνταῦθα τὴν ὁμοίωσιν ἄλλον τρόπον ληπτέον οὐ ταὐτὸν εἶδος ἀπαιτοῦντας, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον ἕτερον, εἴπερ κατὰ τὸν ἕτερον τρόπον ὡμοίωται.

paragraphs.modern: What, then, is virtue, both virtue as a whole and each virtue? The account will be clearer if we take each one, for in this way what they have in common, which makes them all virtues, will easily become plain. The civic virtues, which we spoke of above, really do give order to us and make us better, while we still remain and live here. They do it by setting bounds and measures to our desires, and to our passions in general, and by removing false opinions. They do it by what is altogether better, and by setting bounds, since what has measure stands outside the unmeasured and the unbounded. And the virtues themselves, being bounded, in so far as they are measures in the soul as in matter, have been made like the measure there, and hold a trace of the best that is there. What is wholly without measure is matter, and it is wholly unlike. But in so far as a thing shares in form, it is made like that which is without form. Things nearer share more. Soul is nearer than body and more akin, so it shares more: so much that, appearing as a god, it deceives us into thinking that this is all there is of God. That, then, is how these people are made like God.
paragraphs.greek: τί ποτε οὖν ἐστιν ἡ ἀρετὴ ἥ τε σύμπασα καὶ ἑκάστη; σαφέστερος δὲ ὁ λόγος ἔσται ἐφ̓ ἑκάστης: οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ὅ τι κοινόν, καθ̓ ὃ ἀρεταὶ πᾶσαι, δῆλον ῥᾳδίως ἔσται. αἱ μὲν τοίνυν πολιτικαὶ ἀρεταί, ἃς ἄνω που εἴπομεν, κατακοσμοῦσι μένοντας ἔτι καὶ ἔχοντας ἐνταῦθα καὶ ἀμείνους ποιοῦσιν ὁρίζουσαι καὶ μετροῦσαι τὰς ἐπιθυμίας καὶ ὅλως τὰ πάθη καὶ ψευδεῖς δόξας ἀφαιροῦσαι τῷ ὅλως ἀμείνονι καὶ τῷ ὡρίσθαι καὶ τῶν ἀμέτρων καὶ ἀορίστων ἔξω εἶναι τὸ μεμετρημένον: καὶ αὐταὶ ὁρισθεῖσαι ᾗ μέτρα γε ἐν ὕλῃ τῇ ψυχῇ ὡμοίωνται τῷ ἐκεῖ μέτρῳ καὶ ἔχουσιν ἴχνος τοῦ ἐκεῖ ἀρίστου. τὸ μὲν γὰρ πάντη ἄμετρον ὕλη ὂν πάντη ἀνωμοίωται: καθ̓ ὅσον δὲ μεταλαμβάνει εἴδους, κατὰ τοσοῦτον ὁμοιοῦται ἀνειδέῳ ἐκείνῳ ὄντι. μᾶλλον δὲ τὰ ἐγγὺς μεταλαμβάνει: ψυχὴ δὲ ἐγγυτέρω σώματος καὶ συγγενέστερον ταύτῃ καὶ πλέον μεταλαμβάνει, ὥστε καὶ ἐξαπατᾶν θεὸς φαντασθεῖσα, μὴ τὸ πᾶν θεοῦ τοῦτο ᾖ. οὕτω μὲν οὖν αὗται ὁμοιοῦνται.

flags.taylor: and taking away false opinions from a more excellent nature
flags.why: The Greek says the virtues remove false opinions "by what is altogether better", the means by which they work; it does not say "from a more excellent nature".

flags.taylor: Perhaps, too, these measures are in soul as in matter
flags.why: There is no "perhaps" in the Greek here: the virtues are measures in the soul as in matter.

paragraphs.modern: But since Plato hints that the likeness is a different one, belonging to a greater virtue, we must speak of that. In doing so the being of civic virtue will also become clearer, and what the greater virtue is in its being, and in general that there is another virtue besides the civic. When Plato says that likeness to God is an escape from the things here, and does not call the virtues of civic life simply virtues but adds "civic", and elsewhere calls them all purifications, he plainly holds that virtues are of two kinds, and that the likeness does not come by the civic kind.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐπεὶ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν ἄλλην ὑποφαίνει ὡς τῆς μείζονος ἀρετῆς οὖσαν, περὶ ἐκείνης λεκτέον: ἐν ᾧ καὶ σαφέστερον ἔσται μᾶλλον καὶ τῆς πολιτικῆς ἡ οὐσία, καὶ ἥτις ἡ μείζων κατὰ τὴν οὐσίαν, καὶ ὅλως, ὅτι ἔστι παρὰ τὴν πολιτικὴν ἑτέρα. λέγων δὴ ὁ Πλάτων τὴν ὁμοίωσιν τὴν πρὸς θεὸν φυγὴν τῶν ἐντεῦθεν εἶναι, καὶ ταῖς ἀρεταῖς ταῖς ἐν πολιτείᾳ οὐ τὸ ἁπλῶς διδούς, ἀλλὰ προστιθεὶς πολιτικάς γε, καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ καθάρσεις λέγων ἁπάσας δῆλός τέ ἐστι διττὰς τιθεὶς καὶ τὴν ὁμοίωσιν οὐ κατὰ τὴν πολιτικὴν τιθείς.
notes: "An escape from the things here" is from the Theaetetus (176a-b); the virtues as purifications are in the Phaedo (69b-c); the "civic" virtues are named so in the Republic (430c) and the Phaedo (82a).

paragraphs.modern: In what sense, then, do we call these virtues purifications? And how is it that, once purified, we are made like God most of all? It is like this. The soul is bad when it is mixed up with the body, shares its feelings, and agrees with it in all its opinions. So it would be good, and have virtue, if it did not share the body's opinions but acted alone, and that is to use intellect and to be wise; if it did not share the body's feelings, and that is to be self-controlled; if it did not fear being parted from the body, and that is to be brave; and if reason and intellect led, and the rest did not resist, and that would be justice. Someone who called this state of the soul, in which it thinks and is in this way free from passion, a likeness to God would not be wrong. For the divine is pure, and its activity is such that whatever imitates it has wisdom.
paragraphs.greek: πῶς οὖν λέγομεν ταύτας καθάρσεις καὶ πῶς καθαρθέντες μάλιστα ὁμοιούμεθα; ἢ ἐπειδὴ κακὴ μέν ἐστιν ἡ ψυχὴ συμπεφυρμένη τῷ σώματι καὶ ὁμοπαθὴς γινομένη αὐτῷ καὶ πάντα συνδοξάζουσα, εἴη ἂν ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἀρετὴν ἔχουσα, εἰ μήτε συνδοξάζοι, ἀλλὰ μόνη ἐνεργοῖ: ὅπερ ἐστὶ νοεῖν τε καὶ φρονεῖν: μήτε ὁμοπαθὴς εἴη: ὅπερ ἐστὶ σωφρονεῖν: μήτε φοβοῖτο ἀφισταμένη τοῦ σώματος: ὅπερ ἐστὶν ἀνδρίζεσθαι: ἡγοῖτο δὲ λόγος καὶ νοῦς, τὰ δὲ μὴ ἀντιτείνοι: δικαιοσύνη δ’ ἂν εἴη τοῦτο. τὴν δὴ τοιαύτην διάθεσιν τῆς ψυχῆς, καθ̓ ἣν νοεῖ τε καὶ ἀπαθὴς οὕτως ἐστίν, εἴ τις ὁμοίωσιν λέγοι πρὸς θεόν, οὐκ ἂν ἁμαρτάνοι: καθαρὸν γὰρ καὶ τὸ θεῖον καὶ ἡ ἐνέργεια τοιαύτη, ὡς τὸ μιμούμενον ἔχειν φρόνησιν.

paragraphs.modern: Well then, is not that one also in this state? No: it is not in a state at all; the state belongs to the soul. And the soul thinks in a different way. Of the beings there, one thinks in another way, and the other does not think at all. Then is "thinking" just the same word for two different things? Not at all. One thinks first, and the other thinks in a different way that comes from the first. As speech in the voice is an imitation of the speech in the soul, so the speech in the soul is an imitation of the speech in something else. So, as spoken speech is a copy of the speech in the soul, the speech in the soul, being its interpreter, is a copy of what comes before it. Virtue, then, belongs to the soul. It does not belong to intellect, nor to what is beyond intellect.
paragraphs.greek: τί οὖν; οὐ κἀκεῖνο οὕτως διάκειται; ἢ οὐ διάκειται, ψυχῆς δὲ ἡ διάθεσις. νοεῖ τε ἡ ψυχὴ ἄλλως: τῶν δὲ ἐκεῖ τὸ μὲν ἑτέρως, τὸ δὲ οὐδὲ ὅλως. πάλιν οὖν τὸ νοεῖν ὁμώνυμον; οὐδαμῶς: ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν πρώτως, τὸ δὲ παῤ ἐκείνου ἑτέρως. ὡς γὰρ ὁ ἐν φωνῇ λόγος μίμημα τοῦ ἐν ψυχῇ, οὕτω καὶ ὁ ἐν ψυχῇ μίμημα τοῦ ἐν ἑτέρῳ. ὡς οὖν μεμιμημένος ὁ ἐν προφορᾷ πρὸς τὸν ἐν ψυχῇ, οὕτως καὶ ὁ ἐν ψυχῇ ἑρμηνεὺς ὢν ἐκείνου πρὸς τὸ πρὸ αὐτοῦ. ἡ δὴ ἀρετὴ ψυχῆς: νοῦ δὲ οὐκ ἔστιν οὐδὲ τοῦ ἐπέκεινα.

flags.taylor: is divided when compared with it
flags.why: Taylor has "divided" twice here; Volkmann's Greek has μεμιμημένος, "imitated", and the modern version follows the Greek shown.

notes: The Workshop takes "one" and "the other" of the beings there to be intellect, which thinks in its own way, and the One, which does not think, as the last sentence of the chapter suggests.

paragraphs.modern: We must ask whether purification is the same as this kind of virtue, or whether purification comes first and virtue follows. And does virtue lie in being purified, or in having been purified? Virtue in the process of being purified is less complete than virtue in having been purified, for having been purified is already a kind of goal. But having been purified is the removal of everything foreign, and the good is something other than that. Or, if the soul was good before the purification, is purification enough? Purification will be enough; but what is left will be the good, not the purification. And we must ask what it is that is left. Perhaps the nature that is left was not the good itself, or it would not have come to be in evil. Should we call it good-like, then? Yes, but not able to stay in what is truly good, for it is made so that it can go either way. Its good, then, is to be with what is akin to it, and its evil is to be with the opposite. So it must be with what is akin to it, once it is purified, and it will be with it by turning to it. Does it turn, then, after the purification? Rather, after the purification it has turned. Is this, then, its virtue? Rather, its virtue is what comes to be in it from the turning. What is that? A seeing, and an imprint of what is seen, set in it and at work, as sight is at work on what it sees.
paragraphs.greek: ζητητέον δέ, εἰ ἡ κάθαρσις ταὐτὸν τῇ τοιαύτῃ ἀρετῇ, ἢ προηγεῖται μὲν ἡ κάθαρσις, ἕπεται δὲ ἡ ἀρετή, καὶ πότερον ἐν τῷ καθαίρεσθαι ἡ ἀρετὴ ἢ ἐν τῷ κεκαθάρθαι. ἡ γοῦν ἐν τῷ καθαίρεσθαι ἀτελεστέρα τῆς ἐν τῷ κεκαθάρθαι, τὸ γὰρ κεναθάρθαι οἷον τέλος ἤδη. ἀλλὰ τὸ κεκαθάρθαι ἀφαίρεσις ἀλλοτρίου παντός, τὸ δὲ ἀγαθὸν ἕτερον αὐτοῦ. ἤ, εἰ πρὸ τῆς καθάρσεως ἀγαθὸν ἦν, ἡ κάθαρσις ἀρκεῖ; ἀλλ’ ἀρκέσει μὲν ἡ κάθαρσις, τό δὲ καταλειπόμενον ἔσται τὸ ἀγαθόν, οὐχ ἡ κάθαρσις. καὶ τί τὸ καταλειπόμενόν ἐστι ζητητέον: ἴσως γὰρ οὐδὲ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἦν ἡ φύσις ἡ καταλειπομένη: οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἐγένετο ἐν κακῷ. ἆῤ οὖν ἀγαθοειδῆ λεκτέον; ἢ οὐχ ἱκανὴν πρὸς τὸ μένειν ἐν τῷ ὄντως ἀγαθῷ: πέφυκε γὰρ ἐπ’ ἄμφω. τὸ οὖν ἀγαθὸν αὐτῆς τὸ συνεῖναι τῷ συγγενεῖ, τὸ δὲ κακὸν τὸ τοῖς ἐναντίοις. δεῖ οὖν καθηραμένην συνεῖναι. συνέσται δὲ ἐπιστραφεῖσα. ἆῤ οὖν μετὰ τὴν κάθαρσιν ἐπιστρέφεται; ἢ μετὰ τὴν κάθαρσιν ἐπέστραπται. τοῦτο οὖν ἡ ἀρετὴ αὐτῆς; ἢ τὸ γινόμενον αὐτῇ ἐκ τῆς ἐπιστροφῆς. τί οὖν τοῦτο; θέα καὶ τύπος τοῦ ὀφθέντος ἐντεθεὶς καὶ ἐνεργῶν, ὡς ἡ ὄψις περὶ τὸ ὁρώμενον.

flags.taylor: if the soul was good prior to her impurity
flags.why: The Greek says "before the purification", not "before her impurity".

paragraphs.modern: Did the soul not have these things already, then, and does it not recollect them? It had them, but not at work: they lay stored away, unlit. For them to be lit, and for the soul then to know that they are in it, it must come close to what gives light. And it had not the things themselves but imprints of them, so it must fit the imprint to the true things of which the imprints are imprints. Perhaps this is also why the soul is said to have them: intellect is not foreign to it, and least of all foreign when the soul looks towards it. If it does not, intellect is foreign even when it is present. So too our kinds of knowledge are foreign to us if we never act by them at all.
paragraphs.greek: οὐκ ἄρα εἶχεν αὐτὰ οὐδ’ ἀναμιμνήσκεται; ἢ εἶχεν οὐκ ἐνεργοῦντα, ἀλλὰ ἀποκείμενα ἀφώτιστα. ἵνα δὲ φωτισθῇ καὶ τότε γνῶ αὐτὰ ἐνόντα, δεῖ προσβαλεῖν τῷ φωτίζοντι. εἶχε δὲ οὐκ αὐτά, ἀλλὰ τύπους: δεῖ οὖν τὸν τύπον τοῖς ἀληθινοῖς, ὧν καὶ οἱ τύποι, ἐφαρμόσαι. τάχα δὲ καὶ οὕτω λέγεται ἔχειν, ὅτι ὁ νοῦς οὐκ ἀλλότριος καὶ μάλιστα δὲ οὐκ ἀλλότριος, ὅταν πρὸς αὐτὸν βλέπῃ: εἰ δὲ μή, καὶ παρὼν ἀλλότριος. ἐπεὶ καὶ αἱ ἐπιστῆμαι, ἐὰν μηδ’ ὅλως ἐνεργῶμεν κατ’ αὐτάς, ἀλλότριαι.

flags.taylor: She did not, therefore, possess these, nor recollect them
flags.why: The Greek is a question ("Did it not have them, then, and does it not recollect?"), which the next sentence answers; Taylor makes it a statement.

flags.taylor: when it looks to the illuminating cause
flags.why: The Greek says "when it looks towards it", that is, when the soul looks to intellect; "the illuminating cause" is Taylor's.

paragraphs.modern: We must say how far purification goes, for in this way it will be clear to what the likeness is, and with which god the soul becomes the same. The question is chiefly this: how the soul purifies anger and desire and all the rest, pain and its kin, and how far it can be separated from the body. From the body, perhaps, by drawing itself together, as it were, into its own place; and in any case by being free from passion. It makes the necessary pleasures and the perceptions of the senses only cures and reliefs from pain, so that it is not troubled. It takes away pains, and if it cannot, it bears them calmly and makes them smaller by not feeling with the body. It takes away anger as far as it can, entirely if possible; and if not, at least it does not join in the anger itself, but the involuntary movement belongs to something else, and is slight and weak. Fear it takes away entirely, for it will fear nothing; though here too there may be something involuntary, except where fear serves as a warning.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πόσον ἡ κάθαρσις λεκτέον: οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ἡ ὁμοίωσις τίνι φανερὰ καὶ ἡ ταυτότης τίνι θεῷ. τοῦτο δέ ἐστι μάλιστα ζητεῖν θυμὸν πῶς καθαίρει καὶ ἐπιθυμίαν καὶ τἆλλα πάντα, λύπην καὶ τὰ συγγενῆ, καὶ τὸ χωρίζειν ἀπὸ σώματος ἐπὶ πόσον δυνατόν. ἀπὸ μὲν δὴ σώματος ἴσως μὲν καὶ τοῖς οἷον τόποις συνάγουσαν ἑαυτήν, πάντως γε μὴν ἀπαθῶς ἔχουσαν καὶ τὰς ἀναγκαίας τῶν ἡδονῶν καὶ τὰς αἰσθήσεις. μόνον ποιουμένην ἰατρεύσεις καὶ ἀπαλλαγὰς πόνων, ἵνα μὴ ἐνοχλοῖτο, τὰς δὲ ἀλγηδόνας ἀφαιροῦσαν καί, εἰ μὴ οἷόν τε, πρᾴως φέρουσαν καὶ ἐλάττους τιθεῖσαν τῷ μὴ συμπάσχειν: τὸν δὲ θυμὸν ὅσον οἷόν τε ἀφαιροῦσαν καί, εἰ δυνατόν, πάντη, εἰ δὲ μή, μὴ γοῦν αὐτὴν συνοργιζομένην, ἀλλ’ ἄλλου εἶναι τὸ ἀπροαίρετον, τὸ δὲ ἀπροαίρετον ὀλίγον εἶναι καὶ ἀσθενές: τὸν δὲ φόβον πάντη — περὶ οὐδενὸς γὰρ φοβήσεται: τὸ δὲ ἀπροαίρετον καὶ ἐνταῦθα — πλήν γε ἐν νουθετήσει.

paragraphs.modern: As for desire, plainly the soul will desire nothing base. It will not itself desire food and drink for relaxation, nor sex either. If it does at all, I think it will desire what nature needs, with nothing involuntary in it; and if there is something involuntary, it will go no further than a passing image in the mind. In short, the soul itself will be pure of all these things, and it will want to make the unreasoning part pure too, so that this part is not struck by them; or, if it is, not hard, but its blows will be few and quickly undone by the nearness of reason. It is as if a man lived next door to a wise man and gained from being his neighbour, either by becoming like him, or by being so in awe of him that he dared to do nothing the good man would not want.
paragraphs.greek: ἐπιθυμία δὲ ὅτι μὲν μηδενὸς φαύλου, δῆλον: σίτων δὲ καὶ ποτῶν πρὸς ἄνεσιν οὐκ αὐτὴ ἕξει: οὐδὲ τῶν ἀφροδισίων δέ: εἴ δ’ ἄρα, φυσικῶν, οἶμαι, καὶ οὐδὲ τὸ ἀπροαίρετον ἐχόντων: εἴ δ’ ἄρα, ὅσον μέχρι φαντασίας προπετοῦς καὶ ταύτης. ὅλως δὲ αὐτὴ μὲν πάντως τούτων καθαρὰ ἔσται καὶ τὸ ἄλογον δὲ βουλήσεται καὶ αὐτὸ καθαρὸν ποιῆσαι, ὥστε μηδὲ πλήττεσθαι: εἰ δ’ ἄρα, μὴ σφόδρα, ἀλλ’ ὀλίγας τὰς πληγὰς αὐτοῦ εἶναι καὶ εὐθὺς λυομένας τῇ γειτονήσει: ὥσπερ εἴ τις σοφῷ γειτονῶν ἀπολαύοι τῆς τοῦ σοφοῦ γειτνιάσεως ἢ ὅμοιος γινόμενος ἢ αἰδούμενος, ὡς μηδὲν τολμᾶν ποιεῖν ὧν ὁ ἀγαθὸς οὐ θέλει.

flags.taylor: And as to the desire of meats and drinks for the sake of a remission of pain
flags.why: The Greek has "for relaxation" (anesis); "of pain" is Taylor's addition.

paragraphs.modern: So there will be no struggle. The presence of reason is enough. The worse part will respect it, so that the worse part itself will be vexed if it is moved at all, because it did not keep quiet when its master was there, and it will rebuke itself for its weakness.
paragraphs.greek: οὔκουν ἔσται μάχη: ἀρκεῖ γὰρ παρὼν ὁ λόγος, ὃν τὸ χεῖρον αἰδέσεται, ὥστε καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ χεῖρον δυσχερᾶναι, ἐάν τι ὅλως κινηθῇ, ὅτι: μὴ ἡσυχίαν ἦγε παρόντος τοῦ δεσπότου καὶ ἀσθένειαν ἑαυτῷ ἐπιτιμῆσαι.

paragraphs.modern: None of these things is a sin; they are right conduct for a human being. But our aim is not to be free from sin; it is to be a god. If something of this kind still happens involuntarily, such a person would be a god and a daemon at once, a double being; or rather he would have with him another, who has a different virtue. If nothing of the kind happens, he is a god alone: a god of those who follow the first.
paragraphs.greek: ἔστι μὲν οὖν οὐδὲν τῶν τοιούτων ἁμαρτία, ἀλλὰ κατόρθωσις ἀνθρώπῳ: ἀλλ’ ἡ σπουδὴ οὐκ ἔξω ἁμαρτίας εἶναι, ἀλλὰ θεὸν εἶναι. εἰ μὲν οὖν τι τῶν τοιούτων ἀπροαίρετον γίγνοιτο, θεὸς ἂν εἴη ὁ τοιοῦτος καὶ δαίμων διπλοῦς ὤν, μᾶλλον δὲ ἔχων σὺν αὑτῷ ἄλλον ἄλλην ἀρετὴν ἔχοντα: εἰ δὲ μηδέν, θεὸς μόνον: θεὸς δὲ τῶν ἑπομένων τῷ πρώτῳ.

flags.taylor: but a correction of the man
flags.why: The Greek word (katorthōsis) means right action, doing well; it is not "correction".

notes: "Those who follow" recalls the gods and daemons who follow Zeus in the Phaedrus (246e-247a).

paragraphs.modern: For he himself is the one who came from there, and his own true self, if he became such as he was when he came, is there. Coming here, he was settled together with intellect, and he will make "this" like himself, as far as its power allows, so that, if possible, it is not struck at all, or at least does nothing that does not please its master.
paragraphs.greek: αὐτὸς μὲν γάρ ἐστιν ὃς ἦλθεν ἐκεῖθεν καὶ τὸ καθ̓ αὑτόν, εἰ γένοιτο οἷος ἦλθεν, ἐκεῖ ἐστι: νῷ δὲ συνῳκίσθη ἐνθάδε ἥκων καὶ τοῦτον αὑτῷ ὁμοιώσει κατὰ τὴν δύναμιν τὴν ἐκείνου, ὥστε, εἰ δυνατόν, ἄπληκτον εἶναι ἢ ἄπρακτόν γε τῶν μὴ δοκούντων τῷ δεσπότῃ.

flags.taylor: But coming hither, he will associate with intellect ; and will assimilate this to himself
flags.why: A hard sentence. Volkmann's Greek has "with intellect" (νῷ), as Taylor does; read so, it is not clear what "this" is that the man makes like himself. From what follows ("not struck", "its master") it seems to be the lower part he lives with here. The modern version keeps the Greek shown and marks "this".

paragraphs.modern: What, then, is each virtue for such a man? Wisdom, both theoretical and practical, lies in contemplating what intellect holds; but intellect holds it by direct contact. Each of the two is double: one is in intellect, the other in soul. There it is not virtue; in the soul it is virtue. What is it there, then? Intellect's own activity, and what intellect is. Here, what comes from there and is in another is virtue. For justice itself, and each virtue itself, is not virtue, but a kind of pattern; what comes from it into the soul is virtue. Virtue is the virtue of someone; but each thing itself belongs to itself, and not to anything else.
paragraphs.greek: τίς οὖν ἑκάστη ἀρετὴ τῷ τοιούτῳ; ἢ σοφία μὲν καὶ φρόνησις ἐν θεωρίᾳ ὧν νοῦς ἔχει: νοῦς δὲ τῇ ἐπαφῇ. διττὴ δὴ ἑκατέρα, ἡ μὲν ἐν νῷ οὖσα, ἡ δὲ ἐν ψυχῇ. κἀκεῖ μὲν οὐκ ἀρετή, ἐν δὲ ψυχῇ ἀρετή. ἐκεῖ οὖν τί; ἐνέργεια αὐτοῦ καὶ ὅ ἐστιν: ἐνταῦθα δὲ τὸ ἐν ἄλλῳ ἐκεῖθεν ἀρετή. οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτοδικαιοσύνη καὶ ἑκάστη ἀρετή, ἀλλ’ οἷον παράδειγμα: τὸ δὲ ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἐν ψυχῇ ἀρετή. τινὸς γὰρ ἡ ἀρετή: αὐτὸ δὲ ἕκαστον αὑτοῦ, οὐχὶ δ’ ἄλλου τινός.

flags.taylor: But he will possess intellect by contact
flags.why: The Greek says that intellect has what it holds by direct contact; it does not say that the man possesses intellect.

paragraphs.modern: If justice is doing one's own work, is it always found in a number of parts? Or is there one justice in a number of parts, when there are many parts, and another that is simply doing one's own work, even of a single thing? True justice itself, at any rate, is of one thing towards itself, in which there is not one part and another. So for the soul too, the greater justice is to act towards intellect; self-control is the turning inward towards intellect; and courage is freedom from passion, in likeness to that which the soul looks towards, which is by nature free from passion. In the soul, this freedom comes from virtue, so that it does not share the feelings of the worse partner it lives with.
paragraphs.greek: δικαιοσύνη δὲ εἴπερ οἰκειοπραγία, ἆρα ἀεὶ ἐν πλήθει μερῶν; ἢ ἡ μὲν ἐν πλήθει, ὅταν πολλὰ ᾖ τὰ μέρη, ἡ δὲ ὅλως οἰκειοπραγία, κἂν ἑνὸς ᾖ. ἡ γοῦν ἀληθὴς αὐτοδικαιοσύνη ἑνὸς πρὸς αὑτό, ἐν ᾧ οὐκ ἄλλο, τὸ δὲ ἄλλο: ὥστε καὶ τῇ ψυχῇ δικαιοσύνη ἡ μείζων τὸ πρὸς νοῦν ἐνεργεῖν, τὸ δὲ σωφρονεῖν ἡ εἴσω πρὸς νοῦν στροφή, ἡ δὲ ἀνδρεία ἀπάθεια καθ̓ ὁμοίωσιν τοῦ πρὸς ὃ βλέπει ἀπαθὲς ὂν τὴν φύσιν: αὐτὴ δὲ ἐξ ἀρετῆς, ἵνα μὴ συμπαθῇ τῷ χείρονι συνοίκῳ.

flags.taylor: Hence justice in the soul is to energize in a greater degree intellectually
flags.why: The Greek says that the greater justice of the soul is its activity towards intellect; "greater" belongs to the justice, not to the activity.

paragraphs.modern: These virtues in the soul, then, follow one another, as, there in intellect, do the patterns that come before virtue. For there, thinking is knowledge and wisdom; being turned towards itself is self-control; doing its own work is its justice; and what is like courage is its sameness, its staying pure by itself. In the soul, then, the seeing directed towards intellect is wisdom, theoretical and practical: these are virtues of the soul, for the soul is not these things itself, as intellect is there. The other virtues follow in the same way. And with purification too: since all the virtues are purifications, in the sense of having been purified, the soul must have all of them, or none will be complete. Whoever has the greater virtues necessarily has the lesser ones too, in potential; but whoever has the lesser ones does not necessarily have the greater.
paragraphs.greek: ἀντακολουθοῦσι τοίνυν ἀλλήλαις καὶ αὗται αἱ ἀρεταὶ ἐν ψυχῇ, ὥσπερ κἀκεῖ τὰ πρὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς ἐν νῷ ὥσπερ παραδείγματα. καὶ γὰρ ἡ νόησις ἐκεῖ ἐπιστήμη καὶ σοφία, τὸ δὲ πρὸς αὑτὸν ἡ σωφροσύνη, τὸ δὲ οἰκεῖον ἔργον ἡ οἰκειοπραγία, τὸ δὲ οἷον ἀνδρεία ἡ ταυτότης καὶ τὸ ἐφ̓ αὑτοῦ μένειν καθαρόν. ἐν ψυχῇ τοίνυν πρὸς νοῦν ἡ ὅρασις σοφία καὶ φρόνησις, ἀρεταὶ αὐτῆς: οὐ γὰρ αὐτὴ ταῦτα, ὥσπερ ἐκεῖ. καὶ τὰ ἄλλα ὡσαύτως ἀκολουθεῖ: καὶ τῇ καθάρσει δέ, εἴπερ πᾶσαι καθάρσεις κατὰ τὸ κεκαθάρθαι, ἀνάγκη πάσας ἢ οὐδὲ μία τελεία. καὶ ὁ μὲν ἔχων τὰς μείζους καὶ τὰς ἐλάττους ἐξ ἀνάγκης δυνάμει, ὁ δὲ τὰς ἐλάττους οὐκ ἀναγκαίως ἔχει ἐκείνας.

flags.taylor: and that which is as it were fortitude is immateriality
flags.why: Volkmann's Greek has ταυτότης, "sameness"; Taylor has "immateriality", which is not what the Greek shown says. The modern version follows the Greek.

paragraphs.modern: This, then, is the life that is the chief aim of the good man. Whether he has the lesser or the greater virtues in act, or in some other way, must be looked at virtue by virtue: practical wisdom, for example. If it is going to use other principles, how can the lesser one still remain, even if it is not at work? And what if one virtue by nature goes so far and another so far, and the one self-control sets measures to the passions, while the other takes them away altogether? The same holds for the other virtues, once practical wisdom has been moved. Or perhaps he will know them, and how much he will take from them; and perhaps at times, as circumstances call for it, he will act by some of them. But when he reaches higher principles and other measures, he will act by those. He will not, for example, place self-control in that measure, but will separate himself altogether, as far as he can. And he will not live the life of the good human being that civic virtue thinks right; he will leave it behind and choose another, the life of the gods. For his likeness is to be to them, and not to good human beings. Likeness to good human beings is the likeness of one image to another, each made like the same original. Likeness to the other is likeness to the pattern itself.
paragraphs.greek: ὁ μὲν δὴ προηγούμενος τοῦ σπουδαίου βίος οὗτος: πότερα δὲ ἐνεργείᾳ ἔχει καὶ τὰς ἐλάττους ἢ τὰς μείζους ἢ ἄλλον τρόπον, σκεπτέον καθ̓ ἑκάστην: οἷον φρόνησιν: εἰ γὰρ ἄλλαις ἀρχαῖς χρήσεται, πῶς ἔτι ἐκείνη μένει κἂν εἰ μὴ ἐνεργοῦσα; καὶ εἰ ἡ μὲν φύσει τοσόνδε, ἡ δὲ τοσόνδε, καὶ ἡ σωφροσύνη ἐκεῖνα μετροῦσα, ἡ δὲ ὅλως ἀναιροῦσα; ταὐτὸν δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὅλως τῆς φρονήσεως κινηθείσης. ἢ εἰδήσει γε αὐτὰς καὶ ὅσον παῤ αὐτῶν ἕξει: τάχα δέ ποτε περιστατικῶς ἐνεργήσει κατά τινας αὐτῶν. ἐπὶ μείζους δὲ ἀρχὰς ἥκων καὶ ἄλλα μέτρα κατ’ ἐκεῖνα πράξει: οἷον τὸ σωφρονεῖν οὐκ ἐν μέτρῳ ἐκείνῳ τιθείς, ἀλλ’ ὅλως κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν χωρίζων καὶ ὅλως ζῶν οὐχὶ τὸν ἀνθρώπου βίον τὸν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ, ὃν ἀξιοῖ ἡ πολιτικὴ ἀρετὴ διαζῆν, ἀλλὰ τοῦτον μὲν καταλιπών, ἕτερον δὲ ἀλλαξάμενος τὸν τῶν θεῶν: πρὸς γὰρ τούτους αὐτῷ, οὐ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους ἀγαθοὺς ἡ ὁμοίωσις. ὁμοίωσις δὲ ἡ μὲν πρὸς τούτους, ὡς εἰκὼν εἰκόνι ὡμοίωται ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἑκατέρα. ἡ δὲ πρὸς ἄλλον ὡς πρὸς παράδειγμα.

flags.taylor: For if it uses the other virtues
flags.why: The Greek says "if it is going to use other principles" (archai); Taylor has "the other virtues".

paragraphs.modern: What art, method or practice leads us up to where we must go? Where we must go, to the Good and the first principle, let us take as agreed and as shown by many arguments. And indeed the arguments by which it was shown were themselves a kind of leading up.
paragraphs.greek: Τίς τέχνη ἢ μέθοδος ἢ ἐπιτήδευσις ἡμᾶς οἷ δεῖ πορευθῆναι ἀνάγει; ὅποι μὲν οὖν δεῖ ἐλθεῖν, ὡς ἐπὶ τἀγαθὸν καὶ τὴν ἀρχὴν τὴν πρώτην, κείσθω διωμολογημένον καὶ διὰ πολλῶν δεδειγμένον: καὶ δὴ καὶ δἰ ὧν τοῦτο ἐδείκνυτο ἀναγωγή τις ἦν.

paragraphs.modern: What kind of man must he be who is to be led up? Surely the one who, as Plato says, has seen all things, or most things, and who "at his first birth entered into the seed of a man who will be a philosopher, or a musician, or a lover". The philosopher by nature, the musician and the lover are the ones to be led up. What, then, is the way? Is it one and the same for all of them, or is there one for each? For all of them the journey has two stages: one for those going up, and one for those who have arrived above. The first starts from the things below. The second is for those who are already in the intelligible world and have, as it were, set foot there: they must travel on until they reach the furthest point of the region, which is the end of the journey, when one stands on the summit of the intelligible. But let that wait. Let us first try to speak about the leading up.
paragraphs.greek: τίνα δὲ δεῖ εἶναι τὸν ἀναχθησόμενον; ἆρά γε τὸν πάντα ἢ τὸν πλεῖστά, φησιν, ἰδόντα, ὃς ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ γενέσει εἰσῄει εἰς γονὴν ἀνδρὸς ἐσομένου φιλοσόφου ἢ μουσικοῦ τινος ἢ ἐρωτικοῦ; ὁ μὲν δὴ φιλόσοφος τὴν φύσιν καὶ ὁ μουσικὸς καὶ ὁ ἐρωτικὸς ἀνακτέοι. τίς οὖν ὁ τρόπος; ἆρά γε εἷς καὶ ὁ αὐτὸς ἅπασι τούτοις, ἢ καθ̓ ἕνα ἕκαστον εἷς τις; ἔστι μὲν οὖν ἡ πορεία διττὴ πᾶσιν ἢ ἀναβαίνουσιν ἢ ἄνω ἐλθοῦσιν: ἡ μὲν γὰρ προτέρα ἀπὸ τῶν κάτω, ἡ δέ γε δευτέρα, οἷς ἤδη ἐν τῷ νοητῷ γενομένοις καὶ οἷον ἴχνος θεῖσιν ἐκεῖ πορεύεσθαι ἀνάγκη, ἕως ἂν εἰς τὸ ἔσχατον τοῦ τόπου ἀφίκωνται, ὃ δὴ τέλος τῆς πορείας ἂν τυγχάνει, ὅταν τις ἐπ’ ἄκρῳ γένηται τῷ νοητῷ. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν περιμενέτω, περὶ δὲ τῆς ἀναγωγῆς πρότερον πειρατέον λέγειν.
notes: Plato's words are from the Phaedrus (248d): the soul that has seen most of the realities is born as a lover of wisdom, a lover of beauty, a musician or a lover.

paragraphs.modern: First, then, we must tell these men apart, beginning with the musician, and say what he is by nature. We must take him to be easily moved and excited by beauty, but less able to be moved from within himself; he is ready to respond to whatever strikes him, as it were. As timid people start at noises, so he starts at musical sounds and the beauty in them. He always flees what is out of tune and lacks unity in songs, and pursues what has good rhythm and good shape in rhythms. After these sounds and rhythms and shapes that we perceive, then, he must be led like this. We must separate the matter in which the proportions and ratios are found, and lead him to the beauty that is in them. He must be taught that what excited him was the intelligible harmony and the beauty in it, and beauty as a whole, not only one particular beauty. And the arguments of philosophy must be put into him, by which he is to be led to believe in what he has without knowing it. What these arguments are, we shall say later.
paragraphs.greek: πρῶτον δὴ διασταλτέον τοὺς ἄνδρας τούτους ἡμῖν ἀρξαμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ μουσικοῦ ὅστις ἐστὶ λέγοντας τὴν φύσιν. θετέον δὴ αὐτὸν εὐκίνητον καὶ ἐπτοημένον μὲν πρὸς τὸ καλόν, ἀδυνατώτερον δὲ παῤ αὑτοῦ κινεῖσθαι, ἕτοιμον δὲ ἐκ τῶν τυχόντων οἷον κτύπων, ὥσπερ οἱ δειλοὶ πρὸς τοὺς ψόφους, οὕτως καὶ τοῦτον πρὸς τοὺς φθόγγους καὶ τὸ καλὸν τὸ ἐν τούτοις ἕτοιμον, φεύγοντα ʽδἒ ἀεὶ τὸ ἀνάρμοστον καὶ τὸ μὴ ἓν ἐν τοῖς ᾀδομένοις καὶ ἐν τοῖς ῥυθμοῖς τὸ εὔρυθμον καὶ τὸ εὔσχημον διώκειν. μετὰ τοίνυν τοὺς αἰσθητοὺς τούτους φθόγγους καὶ ῥυθμοὺς καὶ σχήματα οὕτως ἀκτέον: χωρίζοντα τὴν ὕλην ἐφ̓ ὧν αἱ ἀναλογίαι καὶ οἱ λόγοι εἰς τὸ κάλλος τὸ ἐπ’ αὐτοῖς ἀκτέον καὶ διδακτέον, ὡς περὶ ἃ ἐπτόητο ἐκεῖνα ἦν, ἡ νοητὴ ἁρμονία καὶ τὸ ἐν ταύτῃ καλὸν καὶ ὅλως τὸ καλόν, οὐ τό τι καλὸν μόνον, καὶ λόγους τοὺς φιλοσοφίας ἐνθετέον: ἀφ̓ ὧν εἰς πίστιν ἀκτέον ὧν ἀγνοεῖ ἔχων. τίνες δὲ οἱ λόγοι, ὕστερον.

flags.taylor: yet is not disposed to be moved from himself
flags.why: The Greek says he is "less able to be moved from within himself", that is, he needs something outside to move him; Taylor's words come near this.

paragraphs.modern: The lover, whom the musician may turn into, and having turned may either stay as or go beyond, has a kind of memory of beauty. But he cannot grasp it on its own, apart from bodies; struck by the beautiful things he sees, he is excited about them. He must be taught, then, not to fall excited before one body, but must be led by reasoning to all bodies, and shown what is the same in all of them. He must be told that it is other than bodies and comes from elsewhere, and that it is found more in other things: he must be shown beautiful ways of life and beautiful laws (for this already accustoms him to what is lovable in things without body), and that there is beauty in the arts, in the kinds of knowledge and in the virtues. Then all these must be made one, and he must be taught how beauty comes to be in them. From the virtues he must now go up to intellect, to being; and there he must take the upward road.
paragraphs.greek: ὁ δὲ ἐρωτικός, εἰς ὃν μεταπέσοι ἂν καὶ ὁ μουσικὸς καὶ μεταπεσὼν ἢ μένοι ἂν ἢ παρέλθοι, μνημονικός ἐστί πως κάλλους: χωρὶς δὲ ἂν ἀδυνατεῖ καταμαθεῖν, πληττόμενος δὲ ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν ὄψει καλῶν περὶ αὐτὰ ἐπτόηται. διδακτέον οὖν αὐτὸν μὴ περὶ ἓν σῶμα πεσόντα ἐπτοῆσθαι, ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ πάντα ἀκτέον τῷ λόγῳ σώματα δεικνύντα τὸ ἐν πᾶσι ταὐτὸν καὶ ὅτι ἕτερον τῶν σωμάτων καὶ ὅτι ἄλλοθεν λεκτέον καὶ ὅτι ἐν ἄλλοις μᾶλλον, οἷον ἐπιτηδεύματα καλὰ καὶ νόμους καλοὺς δεικνύντα — ἐν ἀσωμάτοις γὰρ ὁ ἐθισμὸς τοῦ ἐρασμίου ἤδη — καὶ ὅτι ἐν τέχναις καὶ ἐν ἐπιστήμαις καὶ ἐν ἀρεταῖς. εἶτα ἓν ποιητέον καὶ διδακτέον, ὅπως ἐγγίνονται. ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἤδη δεῖ ἀναβαίνειν ἐπὶ νοῦν, ἐπὶ τὸ ὄν: κἀκεῖ βαδιστέον τὴν ἄνω πορείαν.
notes: The ascent from one beautiful body to all of them, to ways of life and laws, and to the kinds of knowledge, is Diotima's in Plato's Symposium (210a-d).

paragraphs.modern: The philosopher by nature is ready for it, winged, as it were, and does not need to be separated from bodies as these others do. He is already moving upward, and lacks only someone to show him the way. So he must be shown, and set free, since he wants it himself and has long been free by nature. He must be given mathematics, to accustom him to thinking of what has no body, and to believing in it; and he will take to it easily, since he loves learning. Being virtuous by nature, he must be led on to the completion of his virtues. And after mathematics he must be given the arguments of dialectic, and made, in short, a dialectician.
paragraphs.greek: ὁ δὲ φιλόσοφος τὴν φύσιν ἕτοιμος οὗτος καὶ οἷον ἐπτερωμένος καὶ οὐ δεόμενος χωρίσεως, ὥσπερ οἱ ἄλλοι οὗτοι, κεκινημένος πρὸς τὸ ἄνω, ἀπορῶν δὲ τοῦ δεικνύντος δεῖται μόνον. δεικτέον οὖν καὶ λυτέον βουλόμενον καὶ αὐτὸν τῇ φύσει καὶ πάλαι λελυμένον. τὰ μὲν δὴ μαθήματα δοτέον πρὸς συνεθισμὸν κατανοήσεως καὶ πίστεως ἀσωμάτου — καὶ γὰρ ῥᾴδιον δέξεται φιλομαθὴς ὤν — καὶ φύσει ἐνάρετον ὄντα πρὸς τελείωσιν ἀρετῶν ἀκτέον καὶ μετὰ τὰ μαθήματα λόγους διαλεκτικῆς δοτέον καὶ ὅλως διαλεκτικὸν ποιητέον.

paragraphs.modern: What is dialectic, which must be handed on to the first two as well? It is the state of mind that can say, in reasoned speech, about each thing, what it is, how it differs from other things, and what it has in common with them; among which things it belongs, and where each of these stands; whether it is what it is; how many things there are that are, and again the things that are not, which are other than the things that are. It discusses the good and what is not good, the things that fall under the good and those that fall under its opposite, and what is eternal and what is not; and all of it by knowledge, of course, not by opinion.
paragraphs.greek: τίς δὲ ἡ διαλεκτική, ἣν δεῖ καὶ τοῖς προτέροις παραδιδόναι; ἔστι μὲν δὴ ἡ λόγῳ περὶ ἑκάστου δυναμένη ἕξις εἰπεῖν τί τε ἕκαστον καὶ τί ἄλλων διαφέρει καὶ τίς ἡ κοινότης: ἐν οἷς ἐστι καὶ ποῦ τούτων ἕκαστον καὶ εἰ ἔστιν ὅ ἐστι καὶ τὰ ὄντα ὁπόσα καὶ τὰ μὴ ὄντα αὖ, ἕτερα δὲ ὄντων. αὕτη καὶ περὶ ἀγαθοῦ διαλέγεται καὶ περὶ μὴ ἀγαθοῦ καὶ ὅσα ὑπὸ τὸ ἀγαθὸν καὶ ὅσα ὑπὸ τὸ ἐναντίον καὶ τί τὸ ἀίδιον καὶ τὸ μὴ τοιοῦτον, ἐπιστήμῃ δηλονότι περὶ πάντων, οὐ δόξῃ.
notes: "The things that are not, which are other than the things that are" is the teaching of Plato's Sophist (257b-259b): what is not is not nothing, but what is other.

paragraphs.modern: It stops wandering about the world we perceive and settles in the intelligible world, and does its work there. It lets falsehood go, and feeds the soul in what is called "the plain of truth". It uses Plato's method of division to tell the Forms apart, to find what each thing is, and to find the first kinds; it weaves together, by intellect, the things that come from these, until it has gone through the whole intelligible world; and then, the other way, it takes them apart again, until it comes back to the first principle. Then it is still, since it is at peace in so far as it is there; it no longer busies itself with many things, but has become one, and looks. What is called logic, about propositions and syllogisms, it hands over to another art, as it would the knowledge of how to write. Some of these things it thinks necessary, as coming before the art; but it judges them, as it judges everything else, and thinks some of them useful and others superfluous, belonging to the method that wants them.
paragraphs.greek: παύσασα δὲ τῆς περὶ τὸ αἰσθητὸν πλάνης ἐνιδρύει τῷ νοητῷ κἀκεῖ τὴν πραγματείαν ἔχει τὸ ψεῦδος ἀφεῖσα ἐν τῷ λεγομένῳ ἀληθείας πεδίῳ τὴν ψυχὴν τρέφουσα, τῇ διαιρέσει τῇ Πλάτωνος χρωμένη μὲν καὶ εἰς διάκρισιν τῶν εἰδῶν, χρωμένη δὲ καὶ εἰς τὸ τί ἐστι, χρωμένη δὲ καὶ ἐπὶ τὰ πρῶτα γένη, καὶ τὰ ἐκ τούτων νοερῶς πλέκουσα, ἕως ἂν διέλθῃ πᾶν τὸ νοητόν, καὶ ἀνάπαλιν ἀναλύουσα, εἰς ὃ ἂν ἐπ’ ἀρχὴν ἔλθῃ. τότε δὲ ἡσυχίαν ἄγουσα, ὡς μέχρι γέ του ἐκεῖ εἶναι ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ, οὐδὲν ἔτι πολυπραγμονοῦσα εἰς ἓν γενομένη βλέπει, τὴν λεγομένην λογικὴν πραγματείαν περὶ προτάσεων καὶ συλλογισμῶν, ὥσπερ ἂν τὸ εἰδέναι γράφειν, ἄλλῃ τέχνῃ δοῦσα: ὧν τινα ἀναγκαῖα καὶ πρὸ τέχνης ἡγουμένη, κρίνουσα δὲ αὐτὰ ὥσπερ καὶ τὰ ἄλλα καὶ τὰ μὲν χρήσιμα αὐτῶν, τὰ δὲ περιττὰ ἡγουμένη καὶ μεθόδου τῆς ταῦτα βουλομένης.

flags.taylor: and again, by an analytic process it arrives at that to which it had proceeded from the first
flags.why: The Greek says that it takes things apart again "until it comes to the principle" (archē), the first principle; Taylor's words do not say this.

notes: "The plain of truth" is from the Phaedrus (248b). Plato's method of division is shown in the Sophist and the Statesman; the "first kinds" are the greatest kinds of the Sophist (254b-255e).

paragraphs.modern: But where does this knowledge get its principles? Intellect gives clear principles, if a soul can receive them. Then dialectic puts together, weaves and divides what follows from them, until it arrives at complete intellect. For "it is", as Plato says, "the purest part of intellect and wisdom". Since it is the most valuable of the states of mind in us, it must be concerned with being and with what is most valuable: wisdom with being, and intellect with what is beyond being.
paragraphs.greek: ἀλλὰ πόθεν τὰς ἀρχὰς ἔχει ἡ ἐπιστήμη αὕτη; ἢ νοῦς δίδωσιν ἐναργεῖς ἀρχάς, εἴ τις λαβεῖν δύναιτο ψυχή: εἶτα τὰ ἑξῆς καὶ συντίθησι καὶ συμπλέκει καὶ διαιρεῖ, ἕως ἂν εἰς τέλειον νοῦν ἥκῃ. ʽἔστι γάῤ, φησιν, ʽαὕτη τὸ καθαρώτατον νοῦ καὶ φρονήσεως.ʼ ἀνάγκη οὖν τιμιωτάτην οὖσαν ἕξιν τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν περὶ τὸ ἂν καὶ τὸ τιμιώτατον εἶναι, φρόνησιν μὲν περὶ τὸ ὄν, νοῦν δὲ περὶ τὸ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ ὄντος.
notes: Plato's words are from the Philebus (58d), where Burnet's text has "the pure" (τὸ καθαρὸν) part of intellect and wisdom; Plotinus, as Volkmann prints him, has "the purest". Volkmann's Greek, as First1KGreek gives it, prints "τὸ ἂν" where the sense needs τὸ ὄν, "being".

paragraphs.modern: What, then, is philosophy? The most valuable thing. Are philosophy and dialectic the same? Rather, dialectic is the valuable part of philosophy. We must not think that it is a tool of the philosopher's. It is not bare theorems and rules: it deals with things, and has the things that are as its matter, so to speak. It does go to them by a method, but it holds the things together with the theorems. Falsehood and sophistry it knows only incidentally, when another has made them: it judges falsehood as something foreign, by the truths in itself, and knows, when someone presents it, that it goes against the rule of truth. So it does not know about the proposition as such (that would be like knowing letters); but knowing the truth, it knows what they call a proposition. And in general it knows the movements of the soul: what the soul affirms and what it denies, whether it denies what it affirmed or something else, and whether things are different or the same. It grasps whatever is put before it, as sense-perception grasps things, and leaves exact study of these matters to another art, which enjoys it.
paragraphs.greek: τί οὖν ἡ φιλοσοφία; τὸ τιμιώτατον. ἢ ταὐτὸν φιλοσοφία καὶ διαλεκτική; ἢ φιλοσοφίας μέρος τὸ τίμιον: οὐ γὰρ δὴ οἰητέον ὄργανον τοῦτο εἶναι τοῦ φιλοσόφου: οὐ γὰρ ψιλὰ θεωρήματά ἐστι καὶ κανόνες, ἀλλὰ περὶ πράγματά ἐστι καὶ οἷον ὕλην ἔχει τὰ ὄντα: ὁδῷ μέντοι ἐπ’ αὐτὰ χωρεῖ ἅμα τοῖς θεωρήμασι τὰ πράγματα ἔχουσα: τὸ δὲ ψεῦδος καὶ τὸ σόφισμα κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς γινώσκει ἄλλου ποιήσαντος ὡς ἀλλότριον κρίνουσα τοῖς ἐν αὐτῇ ἀληθέσι τὸ ψεῦδος, γινώσκουσα, ὅταν τις προσαγάγῃ, ὅτι παρὰ τὸν κανόνα τοῦ ἀληθοῦς. περὶ προτάσεως οὖν οὐκ οἶδε — καὶ γὰρ γράμματα — εἰδυῖα δὲ τὸ ἀληθὲς οἶδεν ὃ καλοῦσι πρότασιν, καὶ καθόλου οἶδε τὰ κινήματα τῆς ψυχῆς, ὅ τε τίθησι καὶ ὃ αἴρει, καὶ εἰ τοῦτο αἴρει ὃ τίθησιν ἢ ἄλλο, καὶ εἰ ἕτερα ἢ ταὐτά, προσφερομένων ὥσπερ κατ’ αἴσθησιν ἐπιβάλλουσα, ἀκριβολογεῖσθαι δὲ ἑτέρᾳ δίδωσι τοῦτο ἀγαπώσῃ.

paragraphs.modern: It is the valuable part, then, since philosophy has other parts too. It studies nature, taking help from dialectic, as the other arts make use of arithmetic, though philosophy draws on dialectic more closely. And it studies conduct in the same way, contemplating from there, and adding the habits and the exercises from which the habits come. The habits of reason hold what comes from there as already their own; for most of the moral habits come with matter. The other virtues apply reasoning to particular feelings and actions; but practical wisdom is a kind of reasoning above these, more concerned with the universal: whether the virtues go together, and whether to hold back now or later, or whether something else altogether is better. Dialectic and wisdom, more universally still and without matter, bring everything forward for practical wisdom to use.
paragraphs.greek: μέρος οὖν τὸ τίμιον: ἔχει γὰρ καὶ ἄλλα φιλοσοφία: καὶ γὰρ καὶ περὶ φύσεως θεωρεῖ βοήθειαν παρὰ διαλεκτικῆς λαβοῦσα, ὥσπερ καὶ ἀριθμητικῇ προσχρῶνται αἱ ἄλλαι τέχναι: μᾶλλον μέντοι αὕτη ἐγγύθεν κομίζεται παρὰ τῆς δἱ??ʼλεκτικῆς: καὶ περὶ ἠθῶν ὡσαύτως θεωροῦσα μὲν ἐκεῖθεν, προστιθεῖσα δὲ τὰς ἕξεις καὶ τὰς ἀσκήσεις, ἐξ ὧν προίασιν αἱ ἕξεις. ἴσχουσι δὲ αἱ λογικαὶ ἕξεις καὶ ὡς ἴδια ἤδη τὰ ἐκεῖθεν: καὶ γὰρ μετὰ τῆς ὕλης τὰ πλεῖστα: καὶ αἱ μὲν ἄλλαι ἀρεταὶ τοὺς λογισμοὺς ἐν τοῖς πάθεσι τοῖς ἰδίοις καὶ ταῖς πράξεσιν, ἡ δὲ φρόνησις ἐπιλογισμός τις καὶ τὸ καθόλου μᾶλλον καὶ εἰ ἀντακολουθοῦσι καὶ εἰ δεῖ νῦν ἐπισχεῖν ἢ εἰσαῦθις ἢ ὅλως ἄλλο βέλτιον: ἡ δὲ διαλεκτικὴ καὶ ἡ σοφία ἔτι καθόλου καὶ ἀύλως πάντα εἰς χρῆσιν προφέρει τῇ φρονήσει.

flags.taylor: The rational virtues also have habits, and what are now as peculiarities, which they derive from thence
